reconcile.connective: John Gill reads 'stood' as describing their frozen immobility rather than an upright posture, so it need not exclude an initial fall.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman presses the plain conflict: in Acts 9 the companions stand while Paul falls; in Acts 26 they are all knocked down.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: "The Book of Acts Is Not Reliable! The Negative Case," The Bart Ehrman Blog
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, "The Book of Acts Is Not Reliable! The Negative Case," The Bart Ehrman Blog (March 20, 2024)

excerpts.excerpt_text: stood speechless: astonished and amazed, they had not power to speak one word, nor to rise from the ground, and move one step forward; they were as if they were thunderstruck, and fastened to the earth; for this standing is not opposed to their being fallen to the earth, but to their going forward, and only expresses the surprise and stupidity that had seized them …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill explicitly ties Acts 9:7's 'stood speechless' to Acts 26:14's falling, arguing the standing describes immobility (not resuming an upright stance) and so does not conflict with having fallen.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill's note on Acts 9:7 directly addresses this tension, arguing that 'stood speechless' describes immobility rather than an upright posture and so is compatible with having fallen at Acts 26:14.
